## Step 1: Explain the script

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Map recorded homicides in the Retiro neighbourhood of Buenos Aires in 2023. # <1>
```

1. Start by specifying what the script is designed to produce: a map of recorded homicides in Retiro in 2023. This makes it easier to identify the script if we want to revisit it or use it as the basis for another analysis. See [Organising code with comments](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/05_your_second_crime_map/index.html#sec-comments).

## Step 2: Load packages

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Load packages
pacman::p_load(here, httr2, sf, sfhotspot, tidyverse) # <2>
```

2. `pacman::p_load()` loads the packages needed for this analysis, listed in alphabetical order with the tidyverse package last. **[here](https://here.r-lib.org/)** allows us to specify where to find files in the workspace; **[httr2](https://httr2.r-lib.org)** downloads data from the internet; **[sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/)** handles spatial objects; **[sfhotspot](https://pkgs.lesscrime.info/sfhotspot/)** makes it easy to make crime maps; **[tidyverse](https://tidyverse.tidyverse.org)** provides tools for reading, wrangling and plotting data. Loading packages at the start makes it easy to check which tools the script needs. See [Loading packages](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/02_your_first_crime_map/index.html#sec-loading-packages).

## Step 3: Download the original data

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Download the original data and keep a local copy
request("https://mpjashby.github.io/crimemappingdata/retiro_homicides.csv") |> # <3>
  req_perform(path = here("data", "raw", "retiro_homicides.csv")) # <4>
```

3. `request()` specifies the URL of the file to download. The pipe operator (`|>`) passes that request to the next function. The supplied CSV already contains the recorded homicides for the place and year requested in the exercise, so we do not need to download a larger dataset and filter it. See [Downloading and loading data](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/02_your_first_crime_map/index.html#sec-load-data); [Stringing functions together](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/04_transforming_data/index.html#sec-pipe-operator).
4. `req_perform()` performs the download that was set up by `request()`. `here()` specifies where the original file should be saved, relative to the `crime_mapping` workspace. Keeping an unchanged copy of the original data in `data/raw` means we can return to it if we make a mistake while wrangling the data. See [Keeping your files organised](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/01_getting_started/index.html#sec-create-project).

## Step 4: Read the downloaded data

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Read data
homicides <- here("data", "raw", "retiro_homicides.csv") |> # <5>
  read_csv() # <6>
```

5. `here()` specifies the path to the downloaded CSV file within the workspace. The pipe (`|>`) passes this path to `read_csv()`.
6. `read_csv()` from [readr](https://readr.tidyverse.org) reads the local CSV file from the path passed through the pipe. `<-` stores the result as `homicides`, so that we can refer to those records in the following steps. See [Loading CSV data](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/03_data_wrangling/index.html#sec-data-wrangling-loading-csv-data); [Naming objects](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/03_data_wrangling/index.html#sec-naming-objects).

## Step 5: Convert the data to a spatial object

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Convert longitude and latitude to a spatial object
homicides_sf <- st_as_sf( # <7>
  homicides, # <8>
  coords = c("longitud", "latitud"), # <9>
  crs = "EPSG:4326" # <10>
)
```

7. `st_as_sf()` converts an ordinary object into a spatial object which specifies how the coordinates in the data correspond to locations of the earth, and stores the result as `homicides_sf`. The arguments below tell R how to interpret the coordinate columns. See [Converting data to an SF object](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/05_your_second_crime_map/index.html#sec-your-second-crime-map-converting-our-data-to-an-sf-object).
8. Use the records in `homicides` as the basis of the new spatial object.
9. The coordinate columns have Spanish names. `longitud` contains the x coordinates and `latitud` contains the y coordinates. We must use the actual column names, in that order, rather than translating them into English.
10. `crs = "EPSG:4326"` (_CRS_ means _coordinate reference system_) describes the existing coordinates as longitude and latitude. Assigning this CRS tells R how to translate the numbers in those columns to geographic locations. It's worth noting here that the `crs` argument in `st_as_sf()` _describes_ the coordinate system that the data uses -- in the next step we will _change_ (transform) that coordinate system.

## Step 6: Transform the coordinates

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Transform to a projected coordinate reference system suitable for Buenos Aires
homicides_sf_trans <- st_transform(homicides_sf, crs = "EPSG:5348") # <11>
```

11. `st_transform()` changes the data so that the coordinates are specified using the POSGAR 2007 / Argentina 6 coordinate reference system, a projected CRS that is suitable for mapping Buenos Aires. The result is stored as `homicides_sf_trans`. Remember: `st_as_sf()` _described_ the coordinates already in the file, while `st_transform()` _changes_ them into a different system. See [Transforming the coordinate reference system](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/02_your_first_crime_map/index.html#sec-your-first-crime-map-transforming-the-coordinate-reference-system).

## Step 7: Draw the map

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# Display the map
hotspot_map( # <12>
  homicides_sf_trans, # <13>
  basemap_type = "cartolight", # <14>
  colour = "blue2", # <15>
  size = 3 # <16>
)
```

12. `hotspot_map()` draws the spatial points over a base map. Note that the result of this function is not stored in an object using `<-`, so running it causes the result (in this case, the map) to be displayed directly on the screen. See [Drawing the map](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/02_your_first_crime_map/index.html#sec-drawing-first-map).
13. Specify which object contains the data that we want to map. By this point we've created several objects, so make sure the code here refers to the correct object: `homicides_sf_trans`, not `homicides` or `homicides_sf`.
14. Choose the light `cartolight` style of base map to provide local context without visually competing with the points showing the homicides. See [Base maps](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/07_map_context/index.html#sec-base-maps).
15. Blue points contrast with the light base map, making it easier to identify where the homicides happened. See [Visual hierarchy](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/07_map_context/index.html#sec-visual-hierarchy).
16. Make the points larger than the default, since we want the incidents to be easy to see over the base map. See [Controlling aesthetics](https://books.lesscrime.info/learncrimemapping/2026/05_your_second_crime_map/index.html#sec-aesthetics).
